title: Costmap Layers: What Is Known to Be There, What Was Just Seen, and What Is Too Close to It, Kept Apart so That Each Can Be Cleared Without Losing the Others

questions.question: What question is a costmap built to answer?
options: Is there an obstacle in this cell?
How far is the nearest wall?
May the centre of the vehicle be here?
Which sensor saw this cell last?
questions.explanation: After inflation a cell's cost says whether the vehicle's centre may be there, so the planner need not know the vehicle's size.

questions.question: A wall of 4 m at 0.05 m resolution was how many lethal cells?
questions.explanation: 4 m over cells of 0.05 m, counting both ends. The post of 0.15 m radius was 32 cells.

questions.question: At 0.50 m from a post, with an inscribed radius of 0.25 m and a scale of 3, the cost was:
questions.explanation: Inside 0.25 m it is 253. Beyond, it falls as 252 times e to the minus 3 times the distance past 0.25 m: 216 at 0.30 m, 119 at 0.50 m, 30 at 1 m.

questions.question: The layer that only marks left how many ghost cells when the obstacle went?
questions.explanation: The beams to the wall behind passed through where the obstacle had been. The layer that clears along each beam left 0 ghost cells.

questions.question: Why can the planner treat the vehicle as a point after inflation?
options: The planner's grid is coarser than the vehicle
The gradient keeps it in the middle of free space
The inscribed radius already keeps the centre far enough from every obstacle
The vehicle is small beside the cells
questions.explanation: Every cell within the vehicle's own radius of an obstacle is 253. A centre in any cell below that cannot be touching anything.

questions.question: Why was a gap of 0.40 m closed for a vehicle 0.50 m wide?
options: The gradient made it too costly
The inflation of both posts covers it, so no cell across it is below 253
The posts were merged into one obstacle
The grid was too coarse to show it
questions.explanation: With an inscribed radius of 0.25 m each post closes a quarter of a metre on its side. A gap of 0.60 m left two free cells and one of 0.40 m none.
